 Gaza: Displaced families face flooding and another winter in tents
 Heavy rains have damaged tens of thousands of shelters across the Gaza Strip, according to the United Nations. From Al-Mawasi, near Khan Younis, aid worker Nada Khashan describes the impact on displaced families and the difficulties of maintaining basic healthcare services. 
 By Alessandro Guarasci and Linda Bordoni 
 More than 46,000 households across the Gaza Strip have been affected by heavy rainfall since 6 November, with more than 40,000 family shelters damaged, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
 In its humanitarian situation report published on 13 November, OCHA said that more than 9,000 shelters had reportedly been destroyed beyond repair.
 The flooding has compounded the difficulties facing Palestinians living in displacement sites, where inadequate shelter, damaged infrastructure and shortages of essential supplies are already affecting daily life.
 Speaking to Vatican Radio from Al-Mawasi, near Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip, Nada Khashan , executive director of the Palestinian Human Developmental Association (HuDA), describes how families are struggling to protect themselves from the rain.
 Khashan is herself displaced and works with families living in displacement camps.
 “When it rains heavily, water can come in from underneath and the mattresses, blankets and clothes people depend on can get soaked,” she says. “Think about what that means at night. A parent has to find somewhere dry for their children to sleep.”
 For families living in tents, she explains, finding a dry place to sleep can become the most urgent task of the day, particularly when continued rainfall makes it impossible to dry bedding.
 Listen to an excerpt of the interview with Nada Khashan 
 Flooding and public health risks
 OCHA warns that flooding is creating additional public health risks across Gaza. Rainwater mixing with sewage from damaged networks is exposing residents to contamination, while flooded health facilities and difficult road conditions have disrupted medical services and access for patients.
 According to the UN report, nine health facilities were among those reported damaged by the rainfall. Some health services were suspended because of flooding and difficulties reaching facilities.
 The humanitarian situation is rendered even more critical by shortages of medicines. OCHA reports that approximately 42 per cent of essential medicines were at zero-stock level in October.
 The UN also reports that 85 per cent of assessed households experienced moderate to severe water insecurity, while 66 per cent had access to less than the minimum six litres of drinking water per person per day.
 A displaced Palestinian waits to fetch water   (AFP or licensors)
 Maintaining healthcare services
 HuDA provides food and basic supplies to displaced families, as well as primary healthcare and psychological support activities.
 Patients seek assistance for everyday illnesses, pregnancy check-ups and the management of chronic conditions. However, Khashan says that receiving a medical consultation does not necessarily mean that patients can obtain the treatment they need.
 “A doctor can examine the patient and tell them what they need, but the patient may still struggle to find the medicine, get a test, or reach another facility for specialist care,” she explains.
 The organisation also faces difficulties keeping its services running amid power cuts and shortages of medicines and basic supplies.
 For people with chronic conditions, maintaining continuity of treatment is particularly challenging. They need to obtain medication regularly and return to clinics for follow-up appointments, something, Khashan notes, that becomes increasingly difficult when families are repeatedly displaced.
 Palestinians gather around a fire to keep warm
 Supporting children and families
 A significant part of HuDA's work focuses on children. Its team organises group activities where children can play, spend time with other children and talk about their feelings.
 The organisation also meets directly with families in displacement camps to understand their most urgent needs and identify where assistance can be provided.
 One difficulty adds to another
 Reflecting on the situation in southern Gaza, Khashan says the difficulties facing families cannot be considered separately.
 A family may have already moved several times, only to find that heavy rain has flooded its tent. The following morning, someone in the same family may still need to find a way to reach a health clinic.
 “One of the hardest things,” she concludes, “is how each new difficulty adds to the ones people are already dealing with.”
 Wastewater flows next to tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in Gaza   (DAWOUD ABU ALKAS)
